title: 8259 PIC (Programmable Interrupt Controller)
summary: The 8259 PIC manages hardware interrupts for x86. It has 8 interrupt request lines (IRQ0-IRQ7). Multiple PICs can be cascaded (master + slave) for 15 IRQs. Key registers: ICW1-ICW4 (initialization), OCW1 (interrupt mask), OCW2 (end of interrupt), OCW3 (read status). The PIC prioritizes interrupts (lowest number = highest priority) and provides a vector number to the CPU.

structure.meaning: Initialization: ICW4 needed, single/cascade, edge/level triggered, vector address A7-A5.
Base vector address (bits 7-3). E.g., 0x20 for IRQ0 = vector 0x20.
Cascade configuration: master (which IRQ is connected to slave) or slave (slave ID).
Mode: 8086/8088, auto EOI, buffered mode, special fully nested.
Interrupt Mask Register: bit i = 1 masks IRQ i.
End of interrupt (EOI), rotate priority, set/clear priority.
Read IRR (interrupt request register), read ISR (in-service register), poll command.
Interrupt Request Register: bit i = 1 means IRQ i is pending.
In-Service Register: bit i = 1 means IRQ i is being serviced.

ext.example_decoded: 8259 PIC: ICW1 (edge-triggered, ICW4 needed) to port 0x20
notes: The 8259 PIC is legacy (replaced by APIC in modern systems).
Master PIC: IRQ0-7. Slave PIC: IRQ8-15 (connected to master IRQ2).
Total: 15 IRQs (IRQ2 is used for cascade, not available).
EOI (End of Interrupt) must be sent to the PIC after servicing an interrupt.
APIC (Advanced PIC) replaces 8259 in modern multi-core systems.
